title: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: XDG Autostart Entries
shortTitle: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: XDG Autostart Entries
summary: XDG autostart entries are desktop entry files that a Linux desktop environment reads when a user session starts, and adversaries abuse them by adding or editing such a file so a chosen command runs at every login. Each entry is a small text file with a desktop entry group that includes an Exec directive naming the command or binary to launch, together with metadata such as a display name and icon. System-wide entries live in the shared autostart directory and apply to all users, while per-user entries live in the autostart folder inside the user's configuration directory and need no elevated rights to create. The same files also define default applications for file types and removable media, so an unexpected entry can silently become the handler for content the user opens. Defenders baseline the entries on managed hosts, monitor both directories for newly created files, and inspect the Exec line, because masquerading names and icons are what make a rogue entry hard to spot by eye.

beginner.definition: On Linux, a desktop entry file tells the desktop what to start when you log in. These files use the name ending in dot desktop. An attacker can add one, or change one, so their command runs every time you sign in.
beginner.whyItMatters: The desktop reads these files automatically, so a new entry runs without any warning. A user entry needs only your own account, which means no administrator password is needed. The file is plain text with a friendly name and icon, so it looks like an ordinary application. Many teams review services and scheduled jobs but never look at desktop startup files.
howItWorks: A desktop entry file holds settings, including a directive that names the command to run.
The desktop environment reads every entry in the autostart folders when your session starts.
System-wide entries live in the shared autostart directory and affect all users on the machine.
Personal entries live in the autostart folder inside your home configuration directory.
An attacker adds an entry or changes an existing one so their command runs at login.
Detection compares the entries with a baseline and reads the command line in each file.
beginner.example: Imagine a shared flat where the hallway has a folder marked jobs for the morning. Whoever wakes first reads the notes and does what they say. A visitor slips in a note that says water the plants, but the note actually means open the back door at eight. The housemate follows the note without asking who wrote it.
takeaways: Desktop startup files are a real persistence path on Linux and are easy to overlook.
Check both the shared autostart directory and each user's own autostart folder.
Read the command inside the file, because the display name and icon can be misleading.

objectives: Explain what an XDG autostart entry is and when a Linux desktop reads it.
Locate the system-wide and per-user autostart directories on an XDG compliant desktop.
Describe how the Exec directive in a desktop entry file causes code to run at login.
Detect rogue autostart entries using file integrity monitoring and baseline comparison.
Explain why masquerading makes a malicious entry difficult to notice by appearance alone.
Describe how this sub-technique differs from Windows logon autostart mechanisms.
